subject: Gross et al. (1995)
object: Gross et al. (1995) reported a macrosomic newborn girl with albinism, a black lock of hair at the right temporo-occipital region, retinal depigmentation, and bilateral deafness confirmed by brainstem auditory-evoked potentials. She also had a severe defect of intestinal innervation: biopsy showed aganglionosis of the large intestine and a total absence of neurocytes and nerve fibers in the small intestine, indicating a total lack of sympathetic and parasympathetic innervation. She died of intestinal dysfunction at 5 weeks of age.

subject: Gross et al. (1995)
object: Gross et al. (1995) reported that the proband was the 14th child of consanguineous Kurdish parents. Four of her sibs had the same syndrome and died a few days after birth, and the other 9 sibs were well. The authors concluded that the syndrome represents a new neural crest syndrome with autosomal recessive inheritance.

subject: Gross et al. (1995)
object: Gross et al. (1995) described a syndrome of albinism, black lock, deafness, and a total lack of intestinal neural innervation as a previously unreported neural crest syndrome, and named it ABCD syndrome.

subject: Verheij et al. (2002)
object: Verheij et al. (2002) described ABCD syndrome as an autosomal recessive syndrome characterized by albinism, black lock, cell migration disorder of the neurocytes of the gut (Hirschsprung disease), and deafness. They noted that the phenotype clearly overlaps with Shah-Waardenburg syndrome, which comprises sensorineural deafness, hypopigmentation of the skin, hair and irides, and Hirschsprung disease.

subject: Verheij et al. (2002)
object: Verheij et al. (2002) screened the EDNRB gene in the index patient of the ABCD syndrome family and found a homozygous nonsense mutation in exon 3 (R201X). They suggested that ABCD syndrome is not a separate entity but an expression of Shah-Waardenburg syndrome.

subject: Verheij et al. (2002)
object: Because of the overlap with Shah-Waardenburg syndrome and the finding of a homozygous EDNRB mutation, Verheij et al. (2002) suggested that ABCD syndrome is an expression of Shah-Waardenburg syndrome rather than a separate entity.
